description: We’re EmberTrace, a two-person team combining Python, machine learning, mathematical modelling and frontend development. For Flame in Freefall, we’re building FlameProof to turn NASA’s combustion imagery into traceable measurements and useful research insights. We value scientific accuracy, clear design and reproducible results. We welcome collaborators with experience in computer vision, combustion physics or scientific data analysis.
summary:
EmberTrace is an offline evidence explorer for NASA’s Flame in Freefall challenge. It organizes data from the BASS-II microgravity combustion investigation into an interactive viewer for test records, source videos, and image sequences. Users can inspect the T1 frames and trace how a red luminous feature was measured, search the PSI catalog of 24 combustion investigations, and review the assumptions and source records behind the results. The project also includes images and records for two GMT 175 tests that NASA reported as no ignition.

EmberTrace helps make dispersed combustion evidence easier to inspect and compare, supporting research into fire behavior in spacecraft and future crewed missions. It distinguishes reported facts from interpretation: the T1 image-motion estimate remains provisional, and the catalog’s text matching is a discovery aid, not a safety ranking. This release is an evidence-exploration prototype; it does not yet include a live SI system or validated fire-safety recommendations.
details:
EmberTrace is an offline web app for exploring NASA’s BASS-II microgravity combustion records. It brings together 129 test-matrix rows, an interactive T1 image viewer, source video, a searchable catalog of 24 PSI combustion investigations, and a gallery of 80 additional GMT 175 image previews. Users can move through T1 frames, see the tracked luminous feature alongside its time plot, search investigation descriptions, and open the source and method records behind the results.

The project is designed to make NASA combustion evidence easier to inspect and reuse when studying fire behavior in crewed spacecraft. It prioritizes traceability: reported conditions, derived measurements, assumptions, and unresolved questions are kept distinct. For example, the T1 image-motion estimate remains provisional, and the GMT 175 archive’s 80 available images do not reconcile with the 91 shots listed in the test matrix. The app does not present text matches as hazard rankings or claim validated safety recommendations.

We built the interface with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with Python tools for data preparation, image-preview extraction, reproducibility checks, and file-integrity manifests. The team considered source provenance, units, image timing, calibration, uncertainty, and the limits of interpreting luminous features as physical flame fronts. The result is a transparent evidence-exploration prototype; live SI analysis and expert-validated safety guidance remain future work.
